title: Peddi Made ₹250 Crore. Then Janhvi Kapoor's Leaked Chats Set the Internet on Fire.
excerpt: A box office juggernaut, a director's public apology, leaked WhatsApp screenshots, and the biggest objectification debate Indian cinema has seen in years — the Peddi saga is far from over.
body:
Here is a film that opened to over ₹100 crore in a single day — Ram Charan's first solo release to ever do that — and by its sixth day in theatres, the conversation has nothing to do with box office numbers.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=noatJVfA22U

Peddi crossed ₹250 crore worldwide this week. It became only the second Ram Charan film after RRR to breach the ₹200 crore India gross mark. Director Buchi Babu Sana, who debuted with the quietly devastating Uppena, seemed to have delivered the year's biggest Telugu blockbuster. And then the internet did what the internet does.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZF8i7rv2Sz/

The Scene That Changed Everything

It started with clips. A romantic scene between Ram Charan and Janhvi Kapoor — intense, physical, unmissable — began circulating on social media within 48 hours of release. On its own, a kiss in a film is hardly scandal. But Peddi was sold as a gritty sports drama about a villager who uses kabaddi to unite his community. The steamy sequence felt like it had wandered in from a different movie entirely.

The backlash escalated fast. Viewers zeroed in on Janhvi's character, Achiyamma, arguing that she existed almost exclusively as visual decoration — beautiful, styled within an inch of her life, but with barely any agency in the plot. "Objectification" started trending. Critics, academics, and casual fans all weighed in. Promotional material that emphasised her glamour over her character suddenly looked tone-deaf.

The Director's Apology

Buchi Babu Sana did something rare in Indian cinema: he apologised publicly and confirmed the controversial scenes would be edited out of the theatrical print.

"Cinema grows through its connection with audiences, and as storytellers, we have a responsibility to be mindful of evolving perspectives and sensitivities. Every woman deserves to be respected, valued, and represented with dignity."

It was measured, carefully worded, and — depending on who you ask — either genuinely contrite or strategically timed. What it was not, was common. Directors in Telugu cinema do not typically fold to social media backlash. The fact that Buchi did, and quickly, suggests the noise was loud enough to threaten the film's long-term commercial trajectory.

Then the Chats Leaked

Just when the conversation seemed to be cooling, alleged private messages from Janhvi Kapoor to fan accounts surfaced online. The screenshots, reportedly dating back to October 2025 during production, painted a picture of an actress who had fought back on set.

In one message, Janhvi allegedly wrote: "I told him no boob and waist shots." In another, she claimed Ram Charan himself had intervened on her behalf — that he "yelled at him and said you will not take such angles of her ever again."

The authenticity of the chats hasn't been verified. But verified or not, they've reframed the entire narrative. If Janhvi objected during filming and was overruled, the conversation shifts from "Was she complicit in her own objectification?" to "Was she heard at all?"

Social media, predictably, split down the middle. One camp sees a young actress trying to protect her boundaries in a power-imbalanced industry. The other suspects a well-timed PR manoeuvre designed to separate Janhvi from the controversy while the film continues to print money.

The Bigger Picture

Peddi has now become a case study in what happens when a film's commercial success and its cultural reception diverge completely. The numbers are extraordinary — ₹169 crore India net in five days, #1 in the UK, over $3 million in North America. Ram Charan has delivered. But the conversation around the film will outlast the box office run.

For the diaspora audience watching from the US, UK, and Canada, the Peddi controversy hits a specific nerve. These are viewers who consume both Tollywood spectacle and Western conversations about representation. They're the ones most likely to hold both truths simultaneously: that Peddi is a thrilling, handsomely mounted blockbuster, and that the treatment of its leading lady deserved better.

The film is still running strong in theatres. Ram Charan's star power hasn't dimmed. But Janhvi Kapoor's name is now attached to one of the most significant conversations about women in South Indian cinema this decade. That, more than any opening day number, is what Peddi will be remembered for.
